prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

The plate is headed "inventory", with the standing line "Surveys a shelf of historical PDFs and sorts them by how hard their text will be to recover." beneath it.

The dominant picture, filling roughly half the page, shows A shelf labelled Historical Books holds many PDF volumes. One volume is pulled out and fanned open. A page gauge reading pdfinfo clamps its spine and counts its pages. Six thin slips are drawn from points spread through its thickness: the first page, a tenth, a quarter, half, three-quarters and nine-tenths. Each slip feeds rightward through pdftotext and becomes a strip of extracted text, which heads toward the circles in . A single arrow carries the finished volume on to the sorted piles in .

Magnified circles set beside it show circle one shows a page with at least fifty characters. Circle two shows mostly letters, not symbols. Circle three shows at least ten real words, and beside it a garbled page failing the test. study one shows a filename tag being checked against the pattern. Study two shows a book's title sent first to Internet Archive, then to Gutenberg only if the Archive search found nothing. Study three shows the --skip-online switch bypassing both.

Colour is used so that Green marks easy books and a found online edition. Amber marks medium. Red marks hard, meaning OCR is the only road.

Draw these quantities as dimension marks or counts: six sampled pages per book; three coherence tests (50 characters, 60 percent letters, 10 words); four embedded-text grades; three difficulty grades; two online sources, searched in order; seven in ten good pages earns high, three in ten earns medium.

These trade words appear on the plate, each set against the thing it names: pdfinfo on the page gauge. pdftotext on each slip's passage. embedded text on the extracted strips. high, medium, low, none on the ladder. Internet Archive and Gutenberg on the lookup study. --skip-online on the bypass switch. YYYY - Author - Title.pdf on the filename tag. easy, medium, hard on the piles. inventory.yaml on the output sheet, with or JSON beside it.

Letter these words onto the drawings, spelled exactly as given: Historical Books, each PDF, pdfinfo, pdftotext, page 1, sampled pages, embedded text. 50+ characters, mostly letters, 10+ words, coherent page, garbled page. YYYY - Author - Title.pdf, name checked, Internet Archive, then Gutenberg, --skip-online. easy, medium, hard, inventory.yaml, easiest first, or JSON. high, low, none, online edition found, OCR only.

Set these short notes beside what they explain: Six pages spread through the whole book; Every PDF gets the same survey. Three tests decide whether text is real. Gutenberg searched only when Archive finds nothing; Bad filenames are flagged, not rejected. A worklist for choosing what to mill next. Any online edition makes a book easy; High embedded text is also easy.
